messages.body_plain:
Hello,

A little story time. A few days ago I was building an IRT demonstration using MIRT and I wanted to demonstrate how some specific item parameters function so I generated item parameters and responses using Wingen3. When I estimated the item parameters from the simulated responses I noticed there were a couple of oddly high a1 parameter estimates for a couple of items. I thought this was a little strange so I did a quick little simulation looking at a number of 50 item tests taken by 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000 respondents (100 replications per cell) with dichotomous responses scored through the 3PL to see how well MIRT was recovering parameters. I was a little surprised at what resulted.

>From a correlation standpoint MIRT performs quite well with recovery in the .8-.98 range. However, more surprising to me was when I looked at the deviation between estimated and simulated parameters there is a huge difference in a parameters. On average in each 50 item set a number of items have an a parameter 1 full point higher and a few items with an a parameter 2 points higher. It works out to be 99% of tests are affected by this with 500 responses or less and 74% of tests with 1000 responses. Even with 2000 responses 38% of tests had at least 1 a parameter having a difference of 1 and 12% having a difference of 2. The d and g parameters do not usually exhibit deviations more than 1 point higher.

I put together a table to help explain

                        Parameter Deviations

                        More than 1                              More than 2

                        a          d          g          a          d          g

500       Min       0          0          0          0          0          0

            Max      11        3          0          2          5          0

            Mean    4.05      0.46      0          0.12      1.06      0

            Median 4          0          0          0          1          0

            Mode   4          0          0          0          0          0

            % tests affected           99        39        0          11        64        0

                        Simulated vs Recovered Mean Correlations

                        0.823    0.979    0.683

1000     Min       0          0          0          0          0          0

            Max      5          2          1          1          0          0

            Mean    1.41      0.37      0.12      0.04      0          0

            Median 1          0          0          0          0          0

            Mode   1          0          0          0          0          0

            % tests affected           74        30        12        4          0          0

                        Simulated vs Recovered Mean Correlations

                        0.922    0.990    0.794

2000     Min       0          0          0          0          0          0

            Max      3          2          2          2          0          0

            Mean    0.47      0.22      0.24      0.13      0          0

            Median 0          0          0          0          0          0

            Mode   0          0          0          0          0          0

            % tests affected           38        20        23        12        0          0

                        Simulated vs Recovered Mean Correlations

                        0.954    0.992    0.858

5000     Min       0          0          0          0          0          0

            Max      1          1          1          1          0          0

            Mean    0.11      0.03      0.03      0.01      0          0

            Median 0          0          0          0          0          0

            Mode   0          0          0          0          0          0

            % tests affected           11        3          3          1          0          0

                        Simulated vs Recovered Mean Correlations

                        0.985    0.998    0.930

Here is a link to the table in an excel format: https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/510411/MIRTSimResults.xlsx

What is causing this odd behavior? I spot checked the responses being generated with WinGen3 in MULTILOG and got very similar responses to the simulated results so I don’t believe it’s an issue with how WinGen3 is simulation responses.

Best,

Scott

On Thu, Sep 3, 2015 at 4:39 AM, Scott Withrow <swit...@ku.edu.tr> wrote:
> I can attempt to replicate the issue with simdata. I thought about that first but I wasn't sure how simdata constructed response sets and I couldn't be sure that the problem wouldn't be hidden by conducting the entire simulation with MIRT.

It shouldn't really make much difference what generator is used to make response data. It really is just a matter of constructing expected probability functions and sampling across all possible values weighted by that probability. Just think sample(0:1, 1, prob = c(p0, p1)) repeated for each NxJ element.

simdata() is really just a wrapper to create the internal IRT models defined in mirt, which are then used to generate the expected trace-lines, but of course one could do all this manually (and sometimes you should). In the current dev version you can pass whole mirt objects to the function, so helper functions like mirtCAT::generate.mirt_object are now much more useful, and the whole process seems that much more intuitive.

> In the meantime here are all the files and syntax I used before if you feel like looking through them (https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/510411/MIRTEstTest.7z). WinGen3 is a pretty great item and response set generator available for free (you can Google it if you want to see it's documentation).

Perhaps so, but I have trouble investing in such programs, especially if you are familiar with R (and it looks like WinGen is by the very definition for Windows only, which is another negative for me because I run Linux and Mac OSX). All IRT models can easily be generated and sampled from with a bit of programming, including those not internally defined by the software (in some examples I show how to generate atypical models for item misfit detection reasons, and for generating polynomial latent trait effects. In WinGen and other stand-alone software, I'm not even sure if such things are possible).

Food for thought of course; use whatever software is easiest, most comfortable, and suits the end-goal best. Cheers.

Phil

  # used all response categories or generate a new simulated set

  model1.param <- coef(model1, as.data.frame = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)

  estparam <- data.frame(a1 = model1.param[grepl("*a1", rownames(model1.param)), "par"],

  recovery.cor[i, 2] <- cor(recovery.d)[2]
  recovery.cor[i, 3] <- cor(recovery.g)[2]

Hi Scott,

Okay I see the issue now, and it's actually been known for quite some time in the IRT literature. The problem is that estimating 3PL models via ML is notoriously difficult because the g parameter causes a lot of instability during estimation (often is collinear with the intercept if the item is too easy). ML estimation of 3PL models requires huge samples sizes, which your simulation also appears to be confirming.

One way people tend to get around this issue is to place prior parameter distributions on the estimates to help keep them more stable during estimation. Naturally, this means you are no longer estimation an ML solution but rather a MAP, but the bias introduced is generally thought to be a preventative measure and therefore necessary. I recommend using a normal prior (because of the internal reparameterizations this is the most optimal and intuitive) with a fairly tight SD. Something like this:

###
qlogis(.2) #logit mean
model <- 'F = 1-20
               PRIOR = (1-20, g, norm, -1.38, .5)'
mod <- mirt(dat, model, itemtype = '3PL')
###

HTH.

Phil

If a parameter in a cross-validation set is not uniquely defined, in what sense can you say that you have 'validated' the intercept in the original sample? You may want to simply omit/collapse the sparse category in the original sample to avoid this issue. Otherwise, your results probably won't make any sense (note: there is a way to set the number of unique categories internally with the customK input through the technical list, but just because you can doesn't mean you should). Cheers.

Phil

Apologies if my previous message alluded to a closed-source version of the package. No, I plan to keep future versions public as I find the distribution of quasi-open source packages for R really weird and off-putting.

As an aside about how others choose to develop software, I really can't stop people from modifying the package source code for their own purposes, and I think we all have to respect that some people just don't want their code to be open-sourced (especially at the outset and prior to publication of their ideas). All we can do is hope that after developers are finished writing and publishing they will want to contribute back to open-source projects like mirt. I certainly have used private versions of the code-base in the past for my own work and experiments (and still do) but always with the intention to merge things back if/when they work out. IMHO, not every stage has to publically transparent throughout the writing and process, but I would hope the end-goal is to make it that way after the details/publication specifics are all nailed down. Cheers.

Phil

Hi Virginia,

This is new behaviour for mirt, and was brought to my attention by another user as being non-kosher behaviour for IRT software. Essentially, what has happened is one or more rows in your data contain only NA's and therefore have no observed responses. Vectors like these contribute nothing to the model, have no person fit capability, and do not need to be scored (e.g., you might as well set their ability and precision equal to the mean and SD of the prior when scoring via EAP). So, from here on out these response vectors should be removed entirely.

Here's a quick way to do this:

dat <- subset(dat, rowSums(is.na <http://is.na>(dat)) != ncol(dat))

Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
They both are chi-squared variates where larger values indicate worse fit (the null is always that the data fits). So large values of M2 and S_X2 indicate misfit, and will result in very small p-values; if an item fits well (or in the proper phrasing of how these stats work: there is little evidence to the contrary) then it will have p > .05 or some other cut-off. As for the raw interpretation this is a bit harder, and is why many stats (like in SEMs) are supplemented with other more descriptive statistics, like CFI or RMSEA. For a visual depiction in items it may be useful to check out the itemGAM function to get a better idea of why an item may not be fitting.

Phil

This is part of the problem though, because factor scores are often defined when a vector contains only NA's. For example, when using EAP or MAP estimates a vector of NA's should technically return an estimate with all 0's, where the SEs are equal to the sqrt of the prior variance. So returning NA's for these cases is in fact wrong, but for ML/WLE estimation NA's returned would be more realistic. Same reasoning goes for plausible value imputations where these response patterns are perfectly valid but just add noise to the imputations. So it's not really clear which is better/more correct, therefore I think avoiding this issue altogether is the best route.

I'm not the greatest at creating random data, but below should do the job using graded response model.  It does require arm package for invlogit function. **************
require(arm)
set.seed(1)
N=500 # number cases; N/R unique persons (fully crossed person by rater)
R=5 # number raters
I=10 # number items
head(dat<-data.frame(id=rep(1:(N/R),each=R),rater=rep(1:R,N/R),theta=rep(rnorm(N/R),each = R))) # each person scored by all raters
a <- runif(I,.5,.8)
d1<- runif(I,-2,-1.5)
d2<- d1+runif(I,1,1.4)
d3<- d2+runif(I,1,1.4)
# Generate Random rater effect for each rater (unique for each item)
r <-matrix(rnorm(R*I,0,0.1),R,I)
for (i in 1:I) {
  # Generate cumulative probabilities of graded response model (note intercept due to rater and item)
  dat[,paste0("CumProb",i,".1")] <- with(dat,invlogit(a[i]*theta-d1[i]-r[rater,i]))
  dat[,paste0("CumProb",i,".2")] <- with(dat,invlogit(a[i]*theta-d2[i]-r[rater,i]))
  dat[,paste0("CumProb",i,".3")] <- with(dat,invlogit(a[i]*theta-d3[i]-r[rater,i]))
  # Generate Break Points for in each category by adding width to previous value
  dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".0")] <- 1             -dat$CumProb1.1
  dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".1")] <- dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".0")]+(dat$CumProb1.1-dat$CumProb1.2)
  dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".2")] <- dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".1")]+(dat$CumProb1.2-dat$CumProb1.3)
  # Random variable to select category
  dat$R01 <- runif(N,0,1)
  # Create final Y value
  dat[,paste0("Y",i)] <- ifelse(dat$R01<=dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".0")],0,
                         ifelse(dat$R01<=dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".1")],1,
                         ifelse(dat$R01<=dat[,paste0("Prob",i,".2")],2,3)))

}
dat<-dat[,c("id","rater","theta","Y1","Y2","Y3","Y4","Y5","Y6","Y7","Y8","Y9","Y10")]

Perfect, I see what you are saying now. Unfortunately there doesn't seem to be an easy way to do this in the package, mostly because mixedmirt() doesn't support rating scale items for polytomous data (yet). It's on the todo list, but it's implementation is rather cumbersome.

You could approach the problem slightly differently though through the mirt() function, and it would just require that the data be reorganized into the wide form (where each subject is on only one row). Continuing with your example code, here are three models which increase in the number of constraints imposed on the model (the last one seems to be what you are looking for):

library(reshape2)
mlt <- melt(dat, id.vars = c('id', 'rater', 'theta'))
wide <- dcast(mlt, id + theta ~ rater + variable)
items <- wide[,-c(1:2)]
apply(items, 2, function(x) length(unique(x)))

# extremely loose rating scale model for each item
mod <- mirt(items, 1, 'grsm')
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)

# more constrained, accounting for specific rating effects
model <- 'F=1-50
          FIXED = (1-10, c)
          START = (1-10, c, 0.0)
          CONSTRAIN = (11-20, c), (21-30, c), (31-40, c), (41-50, c)'
mod2 <- mirt(items, model, 'grsm')
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE)

# even more constrained (equal slopes)
# cat(rowSums(expand.grid(c(1,11,21,31,41), 0:9)), sep=',')
model2 <- "F=1-50
           FIXED = (1-10, c)
           START = (1-10, c, 0.0)
           CONSTRAIN = (11-20, c), (21-30, c), (31-40, c), (41-50, c),
             (1,11,21,31,41,a1),(2,12,22,32,42,a1),(3,13,23,33,43,a1),(4,14,24,34,44,a1),
             (5,15,25,35,45,a1),(6,16,26,36,46,a1),(7,17,27,37,47,a1),(8,18,28,38,48,a1),
             (9,19,29,39,49,a1),(10,20,30,40,50,a1)"

mod3 <- mirt(items, model2, 'grsm')
coef(mod3, simplify=TRUE)

anova(mod, mod2)
anova(mod2, mod3)
anova(mod, mod3)

Cheers.

Phil

Hello, Phil.

Can I fit a Thurstonian IRT model with mirt.model()?

messages.body_plain:
In principle I don't see why you couldn't estimate these models in mirt, though for now you'd have to switch to the Rsolnp optimizer to account for the reverse-sign equality constraints in the transformed loadings matrix (what they call $\breve{\Lambda}$). There may be a problem with high-dimensionality as well, but I'm not familiar enough with the models to confirm that.

Otherwise, if you wanted to use the default optimizers for unbounded parameters, I would have to add a 'signed' argument somewhere to indicate that there are equality constraints but that their signs are flipped (i.e., instead of a1_1 = a1_2, it would have to be a1_1 = -a1_2), or more generally a transformation matrix for the entire parameter set (which I already use, but it's generally built up from inputs rather than directly accessible by the user). The latter would be the most general, so I'll probably consider adding that sometime in the future anyway.

Phil

Hi Phil,

I am trying to asses the differential item functioning using multigroup and there are a few things that cannot quite grasp:

I'm running a two factors model

s2 <- 'F1 = 1-5
F2 = 6-9'
m2 <- mirt.model(s2)
two_factors <- multipleGroup(dat, m2, group = year, invariance= c('free_var', 'free_means'),
                       survey.weights= weights)

And then, because I want  to explore the evolution over time (hence, group=year) of the factors, I think I need to make sure that the metric model is not significantly worse than the "free" model.
To do so, I'd constrain the loadings/slopes to be equal across years because I need the factors' structure to be consistent. However, I'd want the thresholds/intercepts to be free because I expect some change in the way in which people answer the questions (these are attitudinal survey data).Therefore I'm not concerned about the scalar invariance or the configural invariance. Am I right until now?

So, if the above was the "free" model, I would run the metric model as follows:

metric_model <- multipleGroup(dat, m2, group = year, invariance= c('free_var', 'free_means', 'slopes'),
                             survey.weights= peso)

However, following the examples from the mirt's pdf file, the metric model would be:

mod_metric <- multipleGroup( data, m2, group = year, invariance=c('slopes'), #equal slopes
                            survey.weights= peso)

But wouldn't this constrain the factors' mean and variance to be the same? If I want to look at the variation in the factors, shouldn't I allow the mean and variance to be free (except for the reference group)?

Thank you very much.

Virginia

You might want something more like this for longitudinal IRT models: http://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/Longitudinal-IRT.html. Phil
